title: Peter's Confession and the Way of the Cross
summary: Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven, and Jesus warns his disciples against their leaven, which the disciples finally grasp is their teaching. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God; Jesus blesses him, says that on this rock he will build his church, and promises him the keys of the kingdom. Jesus then begins to teach that he must suffer, die, and rise, calls Peter's protest the voice of Satan, and summons every follower to deny himself and take up his cross.
story:
This chapter is the hinge of Matthew's Gospel. Everything so far has raised the question of who Jesus is: the crowds guess, the leaders accuse, the disciples wonder aloud whether even wind and waves obey him (8:27), and in 14:33 they worship him as the Son of God after he walks on the water. Now, far to the north of the crowds, Jesus asks the question directly and Peter answers it for the others. The phrase “From that time on Jesus began” (verse 21) marks a turn, echoing 4:17, where the same words opened his public preaching. From here the Gospel moves toward Jerusalem and the cross, and every chapter that follows lives in the shadow of verse 21.

The chapter also closes a sequence that began in chapter 14: two feedings, two scenes on the lake, and repeated clashes with the religious leaders over bread, washing, and signs. The disciples, who were told in 13:11 that the secrets of the kingdom had been given to them, still misunderstand a saying about leaven. Yet they are the ones to whom the Father reveals who Jesus is. They have learned who he is; now they must learn what kind of Messiah he is, and Peter, who gets the first lesson right, gets the second one wrong in the same scene. The founding of the church and the first open prediction of the cross stand side by side, so that the community Jesus builds is from the start a community that follows a crucified Lord.
historical:
The Pharisees and Sadducees appear together here (verses 1, 6, 11, 12), a pairing found mostly in Matthew (3:7 and 16:1-12). They disagreed on much. The Sadducees were a party of priestly and aristocratic families centered on the temple in Jerusalem; Josephus says they accepted only the written laws and rejected the traditions of the fathers that the Pharisees observed (Antiquities 13.297-298), and they denied the resurrection of the dead (22:23; Acts 23:8). The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to the careful keeping of the law, including purity and tithing, and they had wide popular respect. Matthew presents them as a common front of unbelief: their joint demand for ‘a sign from heaven’ (verse 1) asks Jesus to prove himself on their terms, after he has already refused the same request in 12:38-40.

Caesarea Philippi lay about forty kilometers (twenty-five miles) north of the Sea of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, beside the spring at Banias that is one of the sources of the Jordan. A cave there held a shrine to the Greek god Pan, which gave the place its older name, Paneas. Josephus says Herod the Great built a temple of white marble there in honor of Augustus (Jewish War 1.404-406; Antiquities 15.363-364), and that Herod's son Philip, tetrarch of the region from 4 BC to AD 34, enlarged the town and named it Caesarea for the emperor, with his own name added to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast (Antiquities 18.28; Jewish War 2.168). Where Herod's temple stood is debated: Ehud Netzer and Zvi Uri Maoz proposed structures at Banias itself, while Andrew Overman, excavating since 1999 at Omrit a few kilometers to the southwest, argued that the temple there is Herod's Augusteum. Either way, the district was thoroughly Gentile, marked by pagan worship and imperial loyalty. Matthew says only that Jesus came into ‘the region’ of Caesarea Philippi (verse 13), not into the city.

The answers of verse 14 reflect real expectations. Herod Antipas had already wondered whether Jesus was John the Baptist raised from the dead (14:1-2). Elijah was expected before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5-6), and Ben Sira, writing in Jerusalem around 180 BC, says Elijah is ready at the appointed time to restore the tribes of Jacob (Sirach 48:10). Only Matthew adds Jeremiah. Jewish writings of the period gave Jeremiah an afterlife as a heavenly intercessor: in 2 Maccabees 15:13-16, Judas Maccabeus dreams of Jeremiah handing him a golden sword, and a later Christian addition to 4 Ezra (2 Esdras 2:18) promises that God will send Isaiah and Jeremiah to help his people. Jeremiah was also the prophet of rejection and suffering who warned of the temple's fall, which may be why the name suggested itself to people watching Jesus.

Crucifixion, which verse 24 assumes, was Rome's punishment for slaves, bandits, and rebels, carried out publicly as a warning. After Herod the Great's death in 4 BC, the Roman governor of Syria, Varus, put down a revolt that reached Galilee and crucified about two thousand men (Antiquities 17.295; Jewish War 2.75). A condemned man usually carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. For Galilean hearers the phrase ‘take up his cross’ was not a figure of speech for inconvenience; it was a picture they had seen.
cultural:
Leaven was a lump of fermented dough kept back from one batch to raise the next. Because a small amount works through the whole, it was an image of influence, good or bad; in 13:33 Jesus uses it for the kingdom's hidden growth. At Passover every trace of leaven was removed from the house (Exodus 12:15-20), so it often stood for corruption, as in Paul (1 Corinthians 5:6-8; Galatians 5:9). Mark has ‘the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod’ (Mark 8:15) and Luke glosses it as hypocrisy (Luke 12:1); Matthew alone explains that Jesus meant ‘the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees’ (verse 12). The reading of the sky in verses 2 and 3 matches weather lore still repeated in many languages: a red sky at evening promised fair weather, a red and lowering sky at morning a storm.

Simon is called Bar-Jonah (verse 17), Aramaic for son of Jonah; John's Gospel calls his father John (John 1:42; 21:15-17), and the two names may be forms of one name or John may preserve the fuller form. The phrase ‘flesh and blood’ was a common Jewish expression for a human being in contrast to God (Sirach 14:18; Galatians 1:16), so verse 17 says Peter's insight did not come from any human source. The name Peter translates the Aramaic kepha, rock or stone, which the New Testament transliterates as Cephas nine times (John 1:42; 1 Corinthians 1:12; Galatians 2:9 among them). Kepha is almost unknown as a personal name before Peter. Joseph Fitzmyer drew attention to a possible instance in an Aramaic papyrus from the Jewish colony at Elephantine in Egypt, a slave sale dated 416 BC whose witness list includes a man described as the son of kp' (Brooklyn Museum papyrus 8, line 10). Either way, a name meaning Rock was striking, the kind of name that invited an explanation.

Keys in the ancient world belonged to a steward who managed a household on the master's behalf and controlled who came in. Isaiah 22:15-25 describes God removing the steward Shebna and giving his office to Eliakim, with the words, “I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open” (Isaiah 22:22); Revelation 3:7 applies the same words to the risen Christ. Binding and loosing were legal and disciplinary terms. In later rabbinic Hebrew, to bind (asar) and to loose (hittir) meant to forbid and to permit under the law, and the Mishnah reports case after case in which the school of Shammai forbids and the school of Hillel permits. The terms could also mean imposing and lifting a ban on a member of the community. Josephus uses the same pair when he says that under Queen Alexandra (76 to 67 BC) the Pharisees became the real administrators of the state, free to banish and recall, to loose and to bind whom they would (Jewish War 1.111).

The gates of Hades (verse 18) is an ancient figure for the power of death. Hades was the Greek name for the realm of the dead, used in the Greek Old Testament for the Hebrew Sheol; it is not the same as Gehenna, the place of final judgment. King Hezekiah, facing death, said he was consigned to the gates of Sheol (Isaiah 38:10); the Wisdom of Solomon says God leads mortals down to the gates of Hades and back again (Wisdom 16:13); and in 3 Maccabees 5:51 the Jews of Alexandria, facing execution, stand at the gates of Hades. To say the gates of Hades will not prevail is to say that death will not hold or defeat what Christ builds. To ‘taste death’ (verse 28) was a Semitic idiom for dying (compare John 8:52; Hebrews 2:9). Peter's protest in verse 22, ‘Far be it from You’, renders an idiom (hileōs soi) that literally means something like ‘God be merciful to you’, a wish that God would spare Jesus such a fate.
literary:
The chapter has two halves, turning on verse 21. In the first (verses 1 to 20), Jesus refuses the leaders a sign, corrects the disciples' literal misunderstanding about bread, and receives Peter's confession. In the second (verses 21 to 28), he predicts his passion for the first time and teaches the cost of following him. Jack Dean Kingsbury (Matthew: Structure, Christology, Kingdom, 1975) argued that the phrase ‘From that time on Jesus began’ at 4:17 and 16:21 divides the whole Gospel into three parts: the person of Jesus, his proclamation, and his suffering, death, and resurrection. Others prefer to outline Matthew by its five great discourses, each closed by the formula ‘When Jesus had finished’ (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1); the two schemes can be held together, and both place this chapter at a turning point.

The second scene with Peter is built as a mirror of the first. Blessed by the Father in verse 17, Peter is addressed as Satan in verse 23. The rock on which the church will be built (petra) becomes a stumbling stone (skandalon) in Jesus' path. His first words came by revelation from the Father in heaven; his second come from ‘the things of men’. Matthew alone records the blessing, the naming, and the promise of the keys (verses 17 to 19), and Matthew alone has Jesus call Peter a stumbling block, so the praise and the rebuke are both sharper here than in Mark 8:27-33 or Luke 9:18-22.

The bread conversation (verses 5 to 12) is a small drama of misunderstanding typical of this section of Matthew. Jesus speaks figuratively; the disciples think literally; Jesus reminds them of the two feedings with the exact numbers of loaves, people, and baskets (14:13-21; 15:32-39); and the narrator reports that they finally understood. Matthew softens Mark's harsher portrait (Mark 8:17-21 ends with the question ‘Do you still not understand?’) by recording their understanding, but he keeps Jesus' rebuke, ‘You of little faith’, his characteristic word for disciples whose trust falters (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). The chapter ends with a double horizon: the Son of Man coming in glory to judge (verse 27) and some standing there who will see him coming in his kingdom (verse 28), a saying Matthew places immediately before the transfiguration, which begins ‘after six days’ (17:1).

outline.t: The leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
Jesus predicts his death; Peter rebuked

doctrines.note: Peter's confession states the heart of Matthew's claim: Jesus is the Christ, the anointed king Israel awaited, and the Son of the living God. Jesus accepts the confession, forbids its public announcement for now (verse 20), and immediately redefines messiahship around suffering, death, and resurrection.

Peter's confession did not come from flesh and blood but was revealed by the Father in heaven (verse 17). Knowing who Jesus is remains God's gift, as in 11:25-27, where the Father hides these things from the wise and reveals them to little children.

This is the first use of the word church in the Gospels. Jesus speaks of it as his own (“My church”), built by him, and promises that the power of death will not prevail against it. How Peter relates to its foundation, and whether any office continues his role, are questions Christians answer differently, set out in the hard questions below.

Jesus says he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and be raised (verse 21). The word must (dei) expresses divine necessity: the cross is not an accident or a defeat but the path God has set, and resisting it is to have in mind the things of men. Matthew will later say why: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28).

Verse 27 promises that the Son of Man will come in his Father's glory with his angels and repay each one according to what he has done, language drawn from Daniel 7:13-14 and from Psalm 62:12. The one who is about to be rejected and killed is the one before whom every person will stand.

words.note: Petra, rock, a mass of bedrock or a cliff; fifteen times in the New Testament, five in Matthew, including the house built on the rock (7:24-25) and the tomb cut in the rock (27:60). Jesus says “you are Peter” (Petros, 155 times in the New Testament) and then “on this rock” (petra). In older and poetic Greek petros often meant a stone and petra a rock mass, but D. A. Carson and others note that by the first century the words overlapped, and petra, being feminine, could not serve as a man's name. In Aramaic the same word, kepha, would stand in both places. What the rock refers to is the chapter's most debated question.

Ekklēsia, assembly or church; about 114 times in the New Testament, but in the Gospels only in Matthew, here and twice in 18:17. In Greek cities it meant the gathered assembly of citizens. In the Greek Old Testament it often translates the Hebrew qahal, the assembly of Israel gathered before God, as at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:10; 9:10). BDAG describes its Christian sense as the congregation or community of those who belong to Christ. Jesus speaks of forming such an assembly around himself, and calls it ‘My’ assembly.

Kleis, key; six times in the New Testament (Matthew 16:19; Luke 11:52; Revelation 1:18; 3:7; 9:1; 20:1). Keys symbolize authority to open and shut, admit and exclude, as with Eliakim the steward in Isaiah 22:22. Jesus later accuses scribes and Pharisees of shutting the kingdom of heaven in people's faces (23:13), and Luke has him say that the lawyers have taken away the key of knowledge (Luke 11:52). Both texts suggest the keys concern opening the way in through teaching the kingdom rightly.

Deō, to bind; about forty-three times in the New Testament, ten in Matthew, paired here and in 18:18 with luō, to loose. Its ordinary sense is physical binding (14:3; 27:2), but the pair bind and loose also served as legal and disciplinary terms for forbidding and permitting, or imposing and lifting a ban. The verbs in verse 19 are periphrastic future perfects, literally ‘will be having been bound’; Julius Mantey argued in 1939 that they mean heaven has already decided what the disciples declare, while Henry Cadbury replied that they are simply future in force. The NASB follows Mantey's rendering.

Hadēs, the realm of the dead; ten times in the New Testament (Matthew 11:23; 16:18; Luke 10:15; 16:23; Acts 2:27, 31; Revelation 1:18; 6:8; 20:13, 14). In the Greek Old Testament it translates Sheol, the grave and the place of the dead, not the place of final punishment (which is Gehenna, 5:22; 18:9). The King James Version renders ‘the gates of hell’, which has led many to read verse 18 as a promise about spiritual warfare; the image is first of all about death, whose gates will not hold what Christ builds, as the risen Christ holds the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18).

Dei, it is necessary, it must; about 101 times in the New Testament, eight in Matthew. Here it governs the whole prediction: the Son of Man must go, suffer, be killed, and be raised. The necessity is not fate but the purpose of God revealed in Scripture, as Jesus says at his arrest: “how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?” (26:54).

Aparneomai, to deny, disown, or renounce; eleven times in the New Testament, all in the first three Gospels. To deny oneself (verse 24) is not to hate oneself or reject one's worth but to disown the self's claim to be master. The same verb describes Peter's denial of Jesus (26:34, 35, 75), so Matthew's readers would feel the irony: the disciple who refused to let Jesus go to the cross later denied his Lord rather than himself.

Skandalon, the trigger of a trap or an obstacle that trips someone; fifteen times in the New Testament, five in Matthew. Jesus tells Peter, “You are a stumbling block to Me” (verse 23): the rock meant for building has become a stone in the road. Paul calls the crucified Christ a skandalon to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23), and 1 Peter 2:8 applies Isaiah's stone of stumbling to Christ himself. Peter's offense is that he tried to trip Jesus away from the cross.

christ:
The chapter is Matthew's clearest statement of who Jesus is and what he has come to do. He is the Christ, Israel's anointed king, the son of David promised in 2 Samuel 7:12-16, and he is ‘the Son of the living God’, a phrase that goes beyond royal title to the unique sonship Jesus has already claimed in 11:27, where no one knows the Son except the Father. God's promise to David was that his son would build a house for God's name (2 Samuel 7:13); here the Son of David says “I will build My church,” a people rather than a building. The link is thematic rather than a direct fulfillment, but it fits Matthew's picture of Jesus as the one greater than the temple (12:6). He also holds the keys: the Christ who promises them to Peter is the one who, in Revelation 3:7, holds the key of David himself.

The Son of Man is at once the glorious figure of Daniel 7, who receives “dominion, glory, and kingship” (Daniel 7:14), and the one who must suffer many things and be killed. Jesus does not quote a text for the ‘must’ in verse 21, but the vocabulary points to Scriptures he cites elsewhere: the rejected stone of Psalm 118:22 (21:42), the servant of Isaiah 53 who is “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3), and the ransom for many (20:28). Raising ‘on the third day’ may recall Hosea 6:2, and it matches the early creed of 1 Corinthians 15:4. These are allusions rather than formal fulfillment formulas, but together they show a Messiah who fulfills Israel's story by suffering on its behalf. The sign of Jonah (verse 4; compare 12:40) points the same way, to the resurrection Jesus now begins to predict openly.

Finally, the chapter shows Christ as judge and as pattern. The one who will be shamed on the cross will come in his Father's glory with his angels and repay each person according to what he has done (verse 27, echoing Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12). And his road becomes his followers' road: the one who loses his life for Jesus' sake will find it (verse 25), the shape of his own death and resurrection laid over theirs. The confession of the church, that the crucified Jesus is Lord and will come again, stands here in seed.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition supplies the nearest parallel to the image of a person as foundation rock. A midrash preserved in the medieval anthology Yalkut Shimoni (on Numbers 23:9) tells of a king who dug for a foundation and found only swamp until he struck rock; so God, looking for a foundation for the world, found Abraham and said he had found a rock (using the Greek loanword petra) on which to build, citing Isaiah 51:1-2, “Look to the rock from which you were cut.” The midrash is later than Matthew, but it shows that calling a faithful person the rock of God's building was intelligible in Jewish idiom.

The church fathers read verses 18 and 19 in more than one way, and often more than one way at once. Tertullian, in On Modesty 21 (early third century, written as a Montanist), insisted that the keys were given to Peter personally and not to a bishop who claimed Peter's power to forgive grave sins. Origen (Commentary on Matthew 12.10-11) taught that every disciple who confesses Christ as Peter did becomes a rock. Cyprian of Carthage's treatise On the Unity of the Catholic Church (251) survives with two versions of chapter 4, a Primacy Text that speaks of a primacy given to Peter and a Received Text that stresses the equal share of all the apostles; the Jesuit scholar Maurice Bévenot argued that both come from Cyprian himself. When Pope Stephen of Rome claimed Peter's succession in the dispute over rebaptism, Firmilian of Caesarea wrote to Cyprian (256; Letter 75 in Cyprian's collection) protesting that Stephen boasted of his see and his succession from Peter while other bishops also stood on the rock. John Chrysostom (Homily 54 on Matthew, around 390) read the rock as the faith of Peter's confession. Augustine at different times read the rock as Peter and as Christ whom Peter confessed, and in his Retractations (1.21) left the reader to choose between the two. Leo the Great, in sermons on the anniversary of his consecration (Sermon 4, in the 440s), taught that the firmness given to Peter continues in his see, and his sermon is still read on the Feast of the Chair of Peter.

The Reformers took the rock as Christ or as the faith Peter confessed. Philip Melanchthon's Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope (1537), now part of the Lutheran Book of Concord, argued that the church is built on the ministry of that confession and that the keys belong to the whole church, and John Calvin answered the Roman claims at length in the Institutes (4.6). The First Vatican Council's constitution Pastor Aeternus (July 18, 1870) cited Matthew 16:16-19 as the ground of a primacy of true and proper jurisdiction given to Peter and continued in the bishop of Rome, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (553, 881) reads the keys as authority to govern the house of God. Orthodox theologians in The Primacy of Peter (1963; revised 1992, edited by John Meyendorff, with essays by Nicholas Afanasiev and Alexander Schmemann) set out the patristic view that Peter's chair belongs to every bishop who holds the apostolic faith. In modern scholarship Rudolf Bultmann judged verses 17 to 19 a creation of the early Palestinian church, while the Protestant Oscar Cullmann (Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr, German 1952, English 1953) defended the saying and argued that the rock is Peter himself, in a foundational role that could not be handed on. John Paul II's encyclical Ut Unum Sint (1995, section 95) invited other churches to help find a way of exercising the primacy open to a new situation.

The chapter is prominent in worship. The Roman lectionary reads Matthew 16:13-19 on the Feast of the Chair of Peter (February 22) and at the Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul (June 29), and 16:13-20 and 16:21-27 on the Twenty-First and Twenty-Second Sundays in Ordinary Time in Year A; the Revised Common Lectionary reads 16:13-20 and 16:21-28 on Propers 16 and 17 in Year A. Anglicans, Lutherans, and others keep the Confession of Saint Peter on January 18, which opens the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Pietro Perugino's fresco Christ Giving the Keys to Saint Peter (1481 to 1482) faces the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, and the Latin of verses 18 and 19 runs in letters taller than a man around the base of the dome of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome. On the second half of the chapter, see the note on Mark 8, where Luther's theology of the cross and Bonhoeffer's The Cost of Discipleship are discussed.
text:
Verses 2b and 3, the sayings about reading the sky from ‘When evening comes’ to ‘the signs of the times’, are missing from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, from several other Greek manuscripts and early versions, and from the text Origen used; Jerome knew that most manuscripts available to him lacked them, though he kept them in the Vulgate. They appear in Codices Ephraemi, Bezae, Regius, and Washingtonianus and in most later manuscripts. The editors of the United Bible Societies' Greek text printed them in brackets and rated the decision as uncertain (Metzger's Textual Commentary). Some think copyists added them from a saying like Luke 12:54-56; others think they were dropped in Egypt, where a red morning sky does not signal rain. Most English Bibles print them, often with a note.

In verse 13 many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘Whom do men say that I the Son of Man am?’, adding ‘me’; modern editions omit it, and the question is about the Son of Man in the third person. Verse 18 is rendered ‘the gates of hell’ (KJV), ‘the gates of Hades’ (BSB, ESV, NASB), and ‘the powers of death’ (RSV, NRSV), three attempts at one Greek phrase. In verse 19 the NASB renders ‘shall have been bound in heaven’ and ‘shall have been loosed in heaven’, reflecting the future perfect form of the Greek (see the note on deō above), while most versions have ‘will be bound’ and ‘will be loosed’. In verse 22 ‘Far be it from You’ (BSB, ESV) and ‘God forbid it’ (NRSV) render an idiom meaning roughly ‘God be merciful to you’. In verses 25 and 26 the same Greek word, psychē, appears as ‘life’ and ‘soul’ in most versions; the NRSV and NIV use ‘life’ throughout. The saying depends on hearing both.

teach.big: The one Peter rightly confesses as Christ and Son of the living God builds his church on that revealed confession and then leads his followers along the road of the cross, where losing life for his sake is the only way to find it.

outline.t: Demanding a sign on our own terms is a refusal to read the signs God has already given; the only sign offered is Jonah's, the death and resurrection of the Son.
Distorted teaching spreads like leaven, and even disciples who have seen Jesus provide twice can forget; remembering his past faithfulness is the cure for anxious literalism.
Everyone must answer ‘Who do you say I am?’, and a true answer is the Father's gift, not human cleverness or achievement.
Christ builds his own church on the rock he names, gives it authority to open the way into the kingdom, and promises that death will not overcome it.
A disciple can confess Jesus rightly and still try to steer him away from the cross; the things of God run through suffering before glory.
Following Jesus means disowning the self's claim to rule, accepting the shame of the cross, and discovering that the self is found only by being given away.
The crucified Son of Man will come as judge and king, and his followers live now in the light of that coming.

teach.pitfalls:
The first pitfall is turning verses 18 and 19 into a weapon. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant readers each have long traditions on this text, and a teacher should state the others' reading in a form its own defenders would accept before giving his own; the text itself is about Christ building his church, a point all three affirm. A second pitfall comes from the King James rendering ‘the gates of hell’, which has led some preachers to picture the church storming hell's fortress. The image may carry that sense, but it first of all concerns death, the realm of Hades, whose gates will not hold Christ's people. A related misuse treats ‘binding and loosing’ as a formula for commanding demons or ‘binding’ circumstances in prayer. In Jewish usage and in Matthew 18:18 the words concern what the community forbids and permits and whom it disciplines and forgives, not incantations.

On the second half, avoid shrinking ‘take up his cross’ into the ordinary troubles of life (a difficult job, a chronic illness, an irritating relative), which hearers often call ‘my cross to bear’. Suffering in general is real and matters to God, but the cross here is the cost of following Jesus, the loss of reputation and life for his sake. Avoid, too, reading self-denial as self-hatred or as the erasure of personality; Jesus promises that the one who loses his life for his sake will find it. Do not use ‘Get behind Me, Satan’ to label opponents in a church dispute: Jesus says it to his closest disciple, who meant well, and the lesson is that loyal-sounding advice can oppose God's purposes. Finally, verse 12 identifies the leaven as the teaching of particular leaders who opposed Jesus; it is not a verdict on Jewish people or on Jewish teaching as such, and Matthew himself praises the scribe trained for the kingdom who brings out treasures new and old (13:52).
teach.pastoral: Verse 24 has been used to tell people in abusive marriages or controlling churches that enduring mistreatment is their cross and that seeking safety is a failure of self-denial. Jesus calls disciples to lose their lives ‘for My sake’ and for the gospel, not to hand themselves over to another person's sin, and the same Gospel commands the protection of the little ones (18:6-10). Teachers should say this plainly, and keep a path to help visible for anyone in danger. The chapter also meets people who fear their faith is too weak or too confused to count. Peter's confession was a gift of the Father, not the prize of a superior mind, and minutes later he was badly wrong; Jesus did not revoke his name. For those who struggle with scrupulosity, the command to deny oneself can become an endless audit of every desire; it is better taught as turning the self over to a trustworthy Lord than as ceaseless suspicion of oneself. And those wounded by the exercise of church authority may hear verse 19 as a threat; it is worth saying that the keys were given to open the kingdom, and that the one who gave them rebuked Peter in the very next scene.

hard.q: What is the rock on which Jesus builds his church, and did Peter's authority pass to successors?
hard.a:
This is a second-order question on which faithful churches divide, and all agree on the first-order point: Christ builds and owns the church, and Peter held a real leading role among the apostles. The strongest challenges come from three directions. The Catholic reading presses Protestants and Orthodox with the grammar: in Aramaic Jesus would have said ‘you are kepha, and on this kepha I will build’, so the rock is most naturally Peter himself, and the keys echo Isaiah 22, where the steward's office passes from Shebna to Eliakim, an office meant to continue. On this basis the First Vatican Council (Pastor Aeternus, 1870) taught that Christ gave Peter a primacy of jurisdiction over the whole church, continued in the bishops of Rome, and Catholic writers point to Leo the Great and others who read the text that way. The Orthodox reading presses in turn that the early church did not understand the text as giving one bishop jurisdiction over the others: Cyprian spoke of one chair of Peter shared by all bishops, Firmilian rebuked Stephen of Rome for boasting of his succession, and Chrysostom read the rock as the faith Peter confessed; Orthodox theologians such as John Meyendorff and Nicholas Afanasiev honor Rome's historic primacy of honor while rejecting universal jurisdiction. Protestants, from Melanchthon's Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope (1537) and Calvin's Institutes (4.6) onward, have read the rock as Christ or the confession of him, citing 1 Corinthians 3:11, “no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.” Many Protestant scholars today, among them Oscar Cullmann and D. A. Carson, accept that the wordplay points to Peter personally, the first to confess and the leader of the first mission (Acts 2; 10), but hold that a foundation is laid once (Ephesians 2:20) and that nothing in the text speaks of successors. A fourth voice is the critical one: Rudolf Bultmann and others judged verses 17 to 19 a saying formed in the early Palestinian church rather than words of Jesus, noting that Mark and Luke lack them.

Each tradition has answers to the others. Catholic writers reply that a foundation stone can be laid once while the office of steward continues, as in Isaiah 22, and that Leo and later Roman bishops read the text in continuity with Peter. Orthodox writers reply that honor and primacy among bishops can be real without jurisdiction over them. Protestant writers reply that Isaiah's steward is a type rather than a charter for succession, and that Galatians 2 shows Paul correcting Peter in public. Defenders of authenticity reply to Bultmann that the Aramaic wordplay, the Semitic phrases ‘flesh and blood’ and ‘Bar-Jonah’, and the unexplained name Cephas in Paul's letters all point to early Palestinian roots. Augustine, who held both that the rock was Peter and that it was Christ, left his readers to choose (Retractations 1.21), and the question remains one of the chief matters of ecumenical dialogue, to which John Paul II invited the other churches in Ut Unum Sint (1995). A reader from any tradition should be able to recognize the other positions here as they are held, and to disagree and remain a brother.

hard.q: Was Jesus mistaken when he said some standing there would not taste death before seeing the Son of Man coming in his kingdom?
hard.a:
The objection is sharper in Matthew than in Mark. Mark speaks of seeing the kingdom of God come with power (Mark 9:1); Matthew speaks of seeing ‘the Son of Man coming in His kingdom’ (verse 28), right after a verse about his coming in glory to judge (verse 27), and Matthew has two similar sayings (10:23; 24:34). Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) built his portrait of Jesus as a prophet of the imminent end on such sayings, and Bertrand Russell, in his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian, cited this very form of the saying as evidence that Jesus expected his return within his hearers' lifetime and was wrong. Many critical scholars hold that the saying preserves an early Christian hope that did not come true.

Christian interpreters have given several answers, which are not mutually exclusive. John Chrysostom (Homily 56 on Matthew) and many after him saw the saying fulfilled six days later in the transfiguration, which Matthew places immediately after it and which 2 Peter 1:16-18 treats as a sight of ‘the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ’. Others see it fulfilled in the resurrection, when the risen Jesus announces that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (28:18), and in Pentecost. R. T. France (The Gospel of Matthew, 2007) argued that Matthew's language of the Son of Man's coming draws on Daniel 7:13-14, where the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive a kingdom, and that it points to his vindication and enthronement, made visible within that generation in the resurrection and in the judgment on the temple in AD 70. Defenders of these readings add that Matthew himself records Jesus saying no one knows the day or hour (24:36), which makes it unlikely that Matthew understood verse 28 as a date for the end. Readers will weigh these answers differently; Matthew's own arrangement shows that he meant the transfiguration to be read as at least a first pledge of the promise.

observe: What do the Pharisees and Sadducees ask for in verse 1, and what sign does Jesus say will be given instead?
What three things does Jesus say to Peter in verses 17 to 19, and what does he tell him in verse 23?
What does Jesus say he must do in verse 21, and what three things does he ask of anyone who wants to come after him in verse 24?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus asks what others say before asking ‘But what about you?’ What is different about Peter's answer?
How can the same disciple be called blessed and then Satan in a few verses? What does that suggest about the difference between confessing Jesus rightly and following him rightly?
What does it mean to lose one's life for Jesus' sake and find it? How does the saying reflect Jesus' own death and resurrection?
apply: If Jesus asked you directly, ‘Who do you say I am?’, how would you answer, and how has your answer changed over time?
Where are you tempted, as Peter was, to want Jesus' power and blessing without his cross?
What would it look like for you, concretely, to deny yourself and follow Jesus this week, and what might you fear losing?
